tweets.text:
The takeaway from this incident should not be that AI is scary. It should be that getting security right is incredibly important in the era of agents. 

Given the right tools and task, agents will do whatever it takes to get the job done, assuming enough compute. Thus, a misconfigured system - or something you thought was locked down but wasn’t - will become a risk vector. 

The core implications are less about the trust and safety of AI itself, but instead the work it’s going to take from enterprises to make sure they harden their environments. Lots of real work ahead for most organizations on this front.

The cost of AI - normalized for the type of task - coming down is one of the most important factors in being able to drive further AI diffusion in the economy.

The general trend we should expect is that frontier AI models will continue to become more capable, and will look very expensive because the tasks that they can take on are more advanced. 

Then, shortly after, AI models will get more efficient or competition will drive more aggressive pricing dynamics, thus reducing the cost per task for anything other than the peak of the frontier.

This cycle will continue over and over again, which ultimately leads to tasks becoming cheaper on a like for like basis. And by doing so you will get even more AI adoption because now AI is more affordable for a wider variety of use-cases.

Great example of how to 6x your accuracy/efficiency by knowing about how the LM you're using in your agents work.

It's always good to be cautious about which harness you use/build for tasks; a lot of tricky little things cause your performance to be drastically different. This time it's context compaction+reasoning format, but there are many others, I've been bitten many times by this.

Partly for this reason recently switched OpenHands to being a "meta-harness" so you can use our agent, or most other agents w/ the same UI/code.

For instance in the agent canvas (https://t.co/vmWqgXf5JA) you can pick other agents and set up an agent profile. My workflow has been to use Codex with gpt-5.6 sol/terra for a lot of things, and glm-5.2 for other things (or if I run out of codex credits), switching agent profiles before each conversation. It's pretty handy!

Or if you're interested in benchmarking you can call the ACP agent in the OpenHands SDK (https://t.co/fOn7MR9EIp). We used this to implement our alternative agents comparison in the OpenHands index here: https://t.co/mCy7wIrnJP

The new Pangram-4 Tech report is out. Some cool details on how to train a SOTA AI-text classifier:

The backbone is an undisclosed “popular open-weight MoE”. Speculating here, but think Mistral Small 4 / Qwen3.5-122B-A10B scale

The authors use LoRA to fine-tune select attention + dense layers, and fully train the classification heads. Fine-tuning the routed experts tanked performance.

A fun trick they use is Repeat2. With a causally masked model you can only see tokens to the left, leaving early predictions context-free. They instead feed [text][text] and score the second copy!

With the recent surge in research on Looped Transformers, we have compiled a list of popular papers tracing the architecture’s development from its earliest forms to its latest iterations.
